unit.name: Theme E: Crime & Punishment
unit.subtitle: Good, evil, crime, punishment and forgiveness

lessons.title: Good, Evil & Reasons for Crime
lessons.description: Good and evil intentions, causes of crime, and religious views on types of crime.
lessons.content_html:
Good and Evil Intentions and Actions

Every action has an intention behind it. Religious believers distinguish between good intentions (those that aim to help others and follow God’s will) and evil intentions (those that aim to harm others or defy what is morally right). A key question in ethics is whether a good intention can justify an action that causes suffering.

Christians believe that God gave humans free will — the ability to choose between good and evil. This means humans are morally responsible for their actions. The Bible teaches: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), suggesting that the world was created good but that humans can choose to act in evil ways.

In Islam, humans are also believed to have free will. Allah created humans as his khalifah (stewards) on earth, responsible for making moral choices. The Qur’an teaches that those who do good will be rewarded on the Day of Judgement, while those who do evil will be held accountable: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it” (Qur’an 99:7–8).

Key Fact

Can it ever be good to cause suffering? Some argue that causing suffering can be justified if it leads to a greater good — for example, a doctor performing painful surgery to save a life, or a parent disciplining a child to teach right from wrong. Others argue that deliberately causing suffering is always wrong because it violates the sanctity of life and human dignity. Christianity teaches “do to others what you would have them do to you” (Matthew 7:12); Islam teaches that Allah is merciful and expects humans to show mercy too.

Reasons for Crime

People commit crimes for many different reasons. Understanding why crime occurs helps society respond appropriately and helps religious believers consider how to balance justice with compassion. the specification identifies four main categories of reasons for crime.

Poverty and upbringing: People living in poverty may steal to feed their families or survive. Those raised in environments where crime is normalised may see it as their only option. Religious believers often show compassion towards people driven to crime by poverty. Jesus taught: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40), encouraging Christians to help the poor rather than simply punish them.

Mental health and addiction: People suffering from mental health problems or addiction may commit crimes because they are not fully in control of their actions. Religious believers may argue that these individuals need treatment and support rather than punishment. Islam teaches compassion for those who are suffering and recognises that people should be judged according to their intentions and circumstances.

Greed and hate: Some crimes are motivated by greed (wanting wealth or power) or hate (prejudice against a group of people). These motivations are generally condemned by religious believers. The Bible warns: “The love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). Islam teaches that greed goes against the principle of zakah — sharing wealth with those in need.

Opposition to unjust laws: Some people break laws they believe are morally wrong — this is called civil disobedience. Rosa Parks broke segregation laws in the USA because she believed they were unjust. Martin Luther King Jr, a Baptist minister, organised peaceful protests against racist laws, arguing that “an unjust law is no law at all” (influenced by St Augustine). Many religious believers support the principle that an immoral law can be legitimately opposed.

Views About People Who Break the Law

Religious believers hold a range of views about lawbreakers. Most agree that breaking the law is wrong, but they differ on how much compassion should be shown and whether the reasons behind the crime matter.

Christians are taught to “hate the sin, love the sinner” — condemning the crime but showing compassion to the criminal. Jesus himself spent time with sinners and outcasts, saying: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick” (Mark 2:17). Islam teaches that humans should show mercy, as Allah is “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman), but also that justice must be upheld — criminals should face appropriate consequences for their actions.

Key Fact

Religious views on lawbreakers depend heavily on the reason for the crime. Someone stealing bread to feed their starving child may receive more sympathy than someone stealing for greed. Someone opposing an unjust law (like Rosa Parks) may be seen as morally right. Both Christianity and Islam balance justice with mercy, teaching that while wrongdoing must have consequences, rehabilitation and forgiveness are also important.

Types of Crime

The exam specification requires knowledge of three specific types of crime and religious views on each.

Hate crimes are offences motivated by hostility towards a person’s identity — their race, religion, sexuality or disability. Both Christianity and Islam condemn hate crimes because they contradict the belief that all humans are created equal by God. The Bible teaches that God “created mankind in his own image” (Genesis 1:27), and the Qur’an states: “We have honoured the children of Adam” (17:70).

Theft is taking what belongs to someone else. It is forbidden by the Ten Commandments (“You shall not steal” — Exodus 20:15) and by the Qur’an. However, some religious believers show compassion towards those who steal out of desperation, while still condemning the act itself.

Murder is the unlawful killing of another person. It is condemned by all religions as a violation of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). The Qur’an teaches: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (6:151).
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about reasons for crime, examiners want to see that you understand the complexity of the issue. Do not simply list reasons — explain how religious believers would respond to each reason with specific teachings. For the 12-mark evaluation, you might consider whether criminals deserve punishment or compassion, using religious evidence to support both sides.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Both Christianity and Islam teach that humans have free will to choose between good and evil, and are accountable for their choices.
  • People commit crimes for different reasons — poverty, mental health, greed, hate and opposition to unjust laws — and religious responses vary depending on the motivation.
  • Hate crimes, theft and murder are all condemned by both religions, but religious believers also teach compassion and the possibility of forgiveness and reformation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar religious beliefs in contemporary British society about why murder is wrong.
In your answer you must refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — the Ten Commandments state 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Christians believe in the sanctity of life — all life is sacred and belongs to God, so taking a life is a sin against God.
• Similarly, Islam teaches that murder is one of the most serious sins. The Qur'an states: 'Do not take life, which God has made sacred' (6:151). Muslims believe that only Allah has the right to give and take life.
• Both religions believe in the sanctity of life and that humans are created by God, making murder a violation of God's authority over life and death.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about whether it can ever be good to cause suffering.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Some Christians argue that causing suffering can be justified if it leads to a greater good — for example, Jesus himself suffered on the cross to save humanity from sin. This suggests that suffering can have a redemptive purpose. The Golden Rule — 'do to others what you would have them do to you' (Matthew 7:12) — suggests we should only cause suffering if we would accept it ourselves for a good reason.
• Islam teaches that Allah is merciful and expects humans to show mercy. Deliberately causing unnecessary suffering goes against this principle. However, the Qur'an acknowledges that suffering can be a test from Allah: 'We shall certainly test you with fear and hunger and loss of property, lives and crops' (2:155). This suggests suffering may serve a divine purpose.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'People who break the law always deserve punishment, not sympathy.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Breaking the law is wrong, and criminals should face consequences to deter others and maintain social order.
• The Bible teaches 'an eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24), suggesting that wrongdoing deserves proportionate punishment.
• Islam teaches that justice must be upheld — the Qur'an describes punishments for crimes like theft, showing that wrongdoing has consequences.
• Without punishment, there would be no deterrent and crime would increase.

Arguments against:
• Jesus taught compassion for sinners: 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick' (Mark 2:17). Christians should show mercy as well as justice.
• People who commit crimes due to poverty, mental health or addiction need help, not just punishment.
• Islam teaches that Allah is 'the most merciful' — Muslims should reflect this mercy in how they treat criminals.
• Rosa Parks broke the law by opposing segregation — her crime was morally right, showing that lawbreaking is not always wrong.
• Reformation (helping criminals change) may be more effective than retribution.

Conclusion: While punishment is necessary to maintain justice and deter crime, religious teachings from both Christianity and Islam emphasise that mercy and understanding are equally important, especially when considering the circumstances behind the crime.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

practice_questions.text:

practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — God 'created mankind in his own image' (Genesis 1:27). This means every person has equal value and dignity. Hate crimes, which target people because of their identity, contradict this belief and are therefore sinful.
• Islam — the Qur'an states 'We have honoured the children of Adam' (17:70), showing that all humans have been given dignity by Allah. Hate crimes violate this principle because they treat certain groups as less worthy. Muhammad's final sermon also emphasised that no race is superior to another.
[6 marks]

lessons.title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty
lessons.description: Aims of punishment, treatment of criminals, and ethical arguments about the death penalty.
lessons.content_html:
The Aims of Punishment

When someone breaks the law, society must decide how to respond. Punishment serves several purposes, and religious believers often disagree about which aim should be prioritised. The three main aims studied in GCSE Religious Studies are retribution, deterrence and reformation.

Retribution means making the criminal “pay” for what they have done. It is based on the idea that wrongdoing deserves a proportionate response. The Old Testament teaches “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21:24), suggesting that punishment should match the severity of the crime. In Islam, the Qur’an records the principle of proportional retaliation as it was ordained for the Children of Israel: ‘We ordained for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye’ (5:45 — a Qur’anic record of a ruling originally given to the Children of Israel in the Torah). Islamic jurisprudence recognises a similar principle of qiṣāṣ (proportional retribution).

Deterrence aims to discourage crime by showing the consequences of breaking the law. If people see that criminals are punished severely, they may be less likely to commit crimes themselves. Both Christianity and Islam support the idea that clear consequences help maintain social order, though they disagree about how harsh those consequences should be.

Key Fact

Reformation focuses on helping criminals change their behaviour and become productive members of society. Many Christians prioritise reformation, following Jesus’s teaching about forgiveness and second chances. The Parable of the Lost Son (Luke 15:11–32) shows God welcoming back those who have strayed, suggesting that criminals can be redeemed. Islam also supports reformation — the Qur’an teaches: “But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness” (5:39).

The Treatment of Criminals

There are several ways in which criminals can be punished. Each method serves different aims and raises different ethical questions.

Prison removes criminals from society to protect the public, and provides time for reformation through education and rehabilitation programmes. However, critics argue that prisons can be “universities of crime,” where offenders learn new criminal skills. Many religious organisations, including Prison Fellowship (a Christian charity), work within prisons to support rehabilitation and spiritual growth.

Corporal punishment means inflicting physical pain on the body — such as caning, flogging or beating. It is banned in the UK but remains legal in some countries. Some Muslims argue that corporal punishment is supported by the Qur’an for certain offences, but others argue that it is outdated and contradicts the principle of mercy. Most Christians oppose corporal punishment, arguing that Jesus taught forgiveness rather than physical retribution.

Community service requires offenders to do unpaid work that benefits the local community. It can serve both deterrence (the offender must give up their time) and reformation (the work may help them develop skills and a sense of responsibility). Many religious believers support community service as a humane alternative to prison, particularly for less serious offences.

The Death Penalty

The death penalty (capital punishment) is the most extreme form of punishment — the state-sanctioned execution of a person convicted of a serious crime. It was abolished in the UK in 1965 but remains legal in many countries, including parts of the USA, China, Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Key Fact

Two key ethical principles apply to the death penalty debate. The principle of utility (utilitarianism) argues that the morality of an action depends on its consequences — if the death penalty deters crime and protects society, it produces the greatest good for the greatest number. The sanctity of life principle argues that all human life is sacred and belongs to God, so no human being has the right to take another’s life, regardless of what they have done.

Arguments for: It acts as the ultimate deterrent — people may be less likely to commit serious crimes if they know they could be executed. It provides retribution — some argue that the most serious crimes (such as serial murder or terrorism) deserve the ultimate punishment. It permanently protects society from the most dangerous criminals. The principle of utility may support it if it saves more lives than it takes.

Arguments against: It violates the sanctity of life — only God has the right to take life. Innocent people may be wrongly convicted and executed, and this cannot be undone. It does not allow for reformation — the criminal can never change or make amends. It reduces the state to the level of the murderer. Evidence suggests that the death penalty does not actually deter crime more effectively than long prison sentences.

Contrasting Beliefs on the Death Penalty and Corporal Punishment

Christianity: Most modern Christian denominations oppose the death penalty. Pope Francis declared in 2018 that the death penalty is “inadmissible” and called for its worldwide abolition. The Church of England also opposes it. Christians argue that Jesus taught forgiveness (“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” — Luke 23:34) and that the death penalty denies the possibility of reformation. However, some Christians point to the Old Testament, which prescribed death for certain offences, as evidence that God sometimes sanctions extreme punishment.

Islam: Islamic law (Shari’ah) permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, including murder and apostasy. However, the Qur’an also encourages mercy: “But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him” (5:45), suggesting that forgiveness is preferred. In practice, many Muslim scholars argue that the conditions for applying the death penalty under Shari’ah are extremely strict and rarely met. Regarding corporal punishment, some forms are prescribed in Islamic law (such as flogging for certain offences), but many modern Muslim scholars argue these should be understood in their historical context.

Key similarity: Both religions teach the sanctity of life and emphasise that mercy and forgiveness are virtues. Both encourage reformation of criminals where possible.

Key difference: Most mainstream Christian denominations now firmly oppose the death penalty, seeing it as incompatible with Jesus’s teachings on forgiveness. Islamic law technically permits it for certain offences, though many Muslim scholars argue that mercy should prevail and that the conditions for its application are extremely difficult to meet in practice.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the death penalty, make sure you can explain both the principle of utility and the sanctity of life arguments clearly. The 12-mark evaluation question often asks you to weigh these two principles against each other. Always include contrasting Christian and Islamic perspectives — note that Christianity generally opposes the death penalty more firmly than Islam, but both emphasise mercy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The three main aims of punishment are retribution (making criminals pay), deterrence (discouraging crime) and reformation (helping criminals change).
  • The death penalty raises key ethical questions about the sanctity of life versus the principle of utility; most Christians oppose it, while Islamic law permits it under strict conditions but encourages mercy.
  • Corporal punishment is banned in the UK but debated in religious contexts — most Christians oppose it, while some Muslims argue it is permitted by Shari'ah under strict conditions.

practice_questions.text:
'The death penalty should be brought back in Britain.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The death penalty acts as the ultimate deterrent — people may be less likely to commit the most serious crimes if execution is a possibility.
• The principle of utility argues that if the death penalty prevents more deaths than it causes, it produces the greatest good for the greatest number.
• Retribution — some argue the most heinous crimes (serial murder, terrorism) deserve the ultimate punishment. The Old Testament prescribed death for certain offences.
• It permanently protects society from the most dangerous criminals.

Arguments against:
• The sanctity of life — both Christianity and Islam teach that all life belongs to God. Only God has the right to take life.
• Jesus taught forgiveness: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). The death penalty contradicts this teaching.
• The death penalty does not allow for reformation — the criminal can never change or make amends.
• Innocent people may be wrongly convicted and executed — this cannot be reversed.
• Pope Francis declared the death penalty 'inadmissible' in 2018.
• Evidence suggests the death penalty does not deter crime more effectively than long prison sentences.

Conclusion: While the death penalty may seem justified for the most serious crimes, religious teachings on the sanctity of life and forgiveness suggest that it is incompatible with the values of both Christianity and Islam. The risk of executing an innocent person makes it particularly problematic.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

However, some Christians cite Proverbs 13:24 ('Whoever spares the rod hates their children') as evidence that physical discipline may sometimes be appropriate.
• Islam — Islamic law (Shari'ah) prescribes corporal punishment for certain offences. However, many modern Muslim scholars argue that these punishments must be understood in their historical context and that the conditions for applying them are extremely strict. The Qur'an also emphasises mercy: 'But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him' (5:45).
[6 marks]

lessons.title: Forgiveness & Corporal Punishment
lessons.description: Religious and non-religious views on forgiveness, its link to justice, and real-world examples.
lessons.content_html:
Forgiveness in Religious Teaching

Forgiveness is one of the most important concepts in both Christianity and Islam. It means pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment or seek revenge. For religious believers, forgiveness is not just a personal choice — it is a moral duty rooted in sacred teaching.

Christianity places forgiveness at the very centre of its faith. Jesus’s death on the cross is understood as the ultimate act of forgiveness — God forgiving humanity for its sins. Jesus taught his followers to forgive others without limit. When Peter asked “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother when he sins against me? Up to seven times?”, Jesus replied: “I tell you, not seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:21–22). This means forgiveness should be unlimited.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer includes the words: “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.” This shows that receiving God’s forgiveness is linked to forgiving others. Christians who refuse to forgive cannot expect God’s forgiveness in return. On the cross, Jesus demonstrated this by praying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described by many names relating to forgiveness, including Al-Ghaffar (“the All-Forgiving”) and Ar-Rahman (“the Most Merciful”). Muslims are taught that forgiving others brings them closer to Allah. The Qur’an states: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). During the month of Ramadan, Muslims are especially encouraged to seek and grant forgiveness.

Non-religious people also value forgiveness, though for different reasons. Humanists may support forgiveness because it promotes human well-being and reduces suffering. Psychologists have shown that holding onto anger and resentment can damage mental and physical health, while forgiveness can lead to healing and improved relationships.

However, some non-religious people argue that forgiveness is not always appropriate. If a criminal has not shown genuine remorse, forgiveness may seem unjust to the victim. Some argue that justice must come before forgiveness — a criminal should face consequences for their actions before any question of forgiveness arises.

Contrasting Beliefs on Forgiveness

Christianity: Most Christians believe that forgiveness is always possible and that believers have a duty to forgive, even when it is extremely difficult. Jesus forgave those who crucified him, setting the ultimate example. However, some Christians distinguish between forgiveness (which is always required) and reconciliation (which may not always be possible or safe). A victim can forgive their attacker without having to re-establish a relationship with them.

Islam: Muslims are encouraged to forgive, but Islam also recognises the right to justice. The Qur’an offers a choice: “The recompense for an injury is an injury equal thereto; but if a person forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40). This means that while forgiveness is preferred and rewarded by Allah, victims also have the right to seek proportionate justice. Some Muslims argue that forgiving is a sign of spiritual strength, while others believe that justice must be served first.

Key Fact

Key contrast: Christianity teaches that forgiveness is unconditional — believers must forgive, even their worst enemies. Islam teaches that forgiveness is highly valued and rewarded by Allah, but it also permits proportionate justice as a legitimate alternative. Both agree that forgiveness leads to reconciliation and is ultimately better for the individual and society.

The Link Between Forgiveness and Justice

One of the most challenging questions in religious ethics is how forgiveness relates to justice. Can you forgive someone while still insisting they face punishment? Most religious believers would say yes — forgiveness is a personal decision about letting go of anger, while justice is about holding people accountable for their actions.

Christians believe that God is both forgiving and just. While God offers forgiveness to all who repent, there are still consequences for sin. The parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46) teaches that people will be judged on their actions. Similarly, in Islam, Allah is both Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) and Al-Adl (the Just) — forgiveness and justice are not contradictory but complementary. A criminal can be forgiven by their victim while still serving a prison sentence, because forgiveness and justice serve different purposes.

Gee Walker: In 2005, Anthony Walker, a Black British teenager, was murdered in a racially motivated attack in Liverpool. His mother, Gee Walker, a devout Christian, publicly forgave her son’s killers. She said: “I can’t hate. I have to forgive them. Unforgiveness makes you a victim, and I refuse to be a victim.” Her forgiveness was inspired by her Christian faith and Jesus’s teaching to forgive others. However, she also supported the killers receiving life sentences — showing that forgiveness and justice can coexist.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa): After apartheid ended in South Africa, Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). Rather than seeking retribution against those who had committed atrocities, the TRC offered amnesty to perpetrators who fully confessed their crimes. Tutu, inspired by his Christian faith, believed that forgiveness and truth-telling were more powerful than punishment in healing a divided nation. He said: “Without forgiveness, there is no future.”

In 2006, a gunman entered an Amish school in Pennsylvania, USA, and killed five girls before taking his own life. The Amish community, deeply committed to their Christian faith, immediately forgave the killer. Members of the community attended the gunman’s funeral and set up a charitable fund for his family. This remarkable act of forgiveness attracted worldwide attention and demonstrated how deeply some Christians take Jesus’s teaching on unlimited forgiveness.

These real-world examples show that forgiveness is not just a theoretical concept — it has transformative power in practice. However, they also show that forgiveness is extremely difficult, especially when the crime is severe. Religious teaching provides a framework for forgiveness, but the personal cost to victims should never be underestimated.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about forgiveness, examiners want to see that you understand the tension between forgiveness and justice. Do not assume they are opposites — religious teaching shows they can coexist. Use specific real-world examples (Gee Walker, Desmond Tutu, the Amish community) to support your arguments. For the 12-mark evaluation, consider whether forgiveness is always possible, or whether some crimes are too severe to forgive.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christianity teaches that forgiveness is an unconditional duty (Matthew 18:21–22), while Islam encourages forgiveness but also permits proportionate justice (Qur’an 42:40).
  • Forgiveness and justice are not opposites — a victim can forgive a criminal while still supporting their punishment, because forgiveness is personal and justice is societal.
  • Real-world examples like Gee Walker, Desmond Tutu’s TRC, and the Amish community demonstrate the transformative power of forgiveness inspired by religious faith.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting religious beliefs in contemporary British society about forgiveness.
In your answer you must refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Jesus taught that forgiveness must be unconditional and unlimited. When asked how many times to forgive, he said 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:22). The Lord's Prayer links receiving God's forgiveness to forgiving others. Forgiveness is a duty, not a choice.
• Islam — the Qur'an encourages forgiveness and promises reward from Allah for those who forgive: 'Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (42:40). However, Islam also permits proportionate justice as a legitimate alternative to forgiveness.
• Key difference: Christianity presents forgiveness as an unconditional duty; Islam values forgiveness highly but gives victims the explicit right to choose between forgiveness and proportionate justice.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the relationship between forgiveness and justice.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Christians believe that God is both forgiving and just. The parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46) teaches that people will be judged on their actions, showing that justice and accountability matter. However, Jesus also taught unlimited forgiveness (Matthew 18:22). Gee Walker forgave her son's killers but also supported their life sentences, showing forgiveness and justice coexisting.
• Islam — Allah is both Al-Ghaffar (the All-Forgiving) and Al-Adl (the Just). The Qur'an teaches: 'The recompense for an injury is an injury equal thereto; but if a person forgives and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (42:40). This shows that justice is permitted, but forgiveness is preferred and rewarded.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'It is always possible to forgive someone, no matter what they have done.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus taught unlimited forgiveness — 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:22). There is no exception mentioned.
• Jesus forgave those who crucified him: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34) — the ultimate example of forgiving the worst possible crime.
• Gee Walker forgave the racially motivated killers of her son, showing that forgiveness is possible even after murder.
• The Amish community forgave the gunman who killed five children in their school.
• The Qur'an promises reward from Allah for those who forgive, regardless of the severity of the crime.
• Forgiveness benefits the victim by freeing them from anger and resentment.

Arguments against:
• Some crimes (genocide, child abuse, terrorism) may be considered too severe to forgive — asking victims to forgive could be seen as trivialising their suffering.
• Forgiveness without justice may send the message that crime has no consequences.
• The victim may not be alive to forgive — can someone forgive on behalf of the dead?
• Islam recognises the right to proportionate justice as a legitimate alternative to forgiveness.
• Humanists may argue that forgiveness depends on the criminal showing genuine remorse.

Conclusion: Religious teaching suggests that forgiveness is always possible in principle, but the reality is that some acts are extraordinarily difficult to forgive. Both Christianity and Islam value forgiveness as a virtue, but they also recognise that it is a deeply personal decision with no easy answers.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]
